sources.design: Systematic review/network meta-analysis of 30 randomized studies and 1,663 participants.
sources.population: De Quervain tenosynovitis; mean age 46 years, 80% women.
sources.outcomes: Adding three to four weeks of thumb-spica immobilization to injection yielded statistically significant but not clinically important functional improvement. No exercise dose established.
sources.uncertainty: Chronicity, reporting and network certainty limit inference; injection findings are not an app exercise prescription.
sources.harms: Procedural harms cannot be assigned to exercise; no generic exercise safety estimate.
sources.limitations: 30 randomized studies/1,663 participants, mean age 46, 80% female; 19 contributed quantitative analyses. Adding thumb-spica immobilization to corticosteroid injection for 3–4 weeks gave statistically significant but not clinically important functional benefits; injection-related treatments dominate evidence. Heterogeneity and low-certainty networks limit rankings. This does not establish exercise dose or prove repetitive thumb movements invariably injurious. Chronicity was inadequately addressed. Injection/splint findings are background clinical context, not an app exercise prescription; procedural harms cannot be attributed to exercise.

sources.design: Four-round Delphi consensus with 35 participating experts; no randomized intervention comparison.
sources.population: People with de Quervain disease, with individual severity, duration and prior treatment considered.
sources.outcomes: Expert advice reduces repetitive or forceful thumb/wrist movement, thumb flexion and ulnar deviation. Static-exercise avoidance conflicts with later isometric feasibility testing.
sources.uncertainty: Expert consensus supplies no tested numeric thresholds; later feasibility data prevent a blanket static-exercise prohibition.
sources.harms: Provocation tests may hurt even healthy people; not evidence that a diagnostic maneuver is a therapeutic stretch.
sources.limitations: Consensus advises individualized instruction alongside treatment. Function-level advice includes reducing repetitive thumb/wrist movement, forceful manual movement, thumb flexion and ulnar deviation. It also lists avoiding static exercises. These are expert recommendations without tested load/angle/duration thresholds, not universal contraindications. Pain-provoking Finkelstein/Eichhoff maneuvers are diagnostic provocations and may also hurt healthy individuals; not automatically therapeutic stretches. The older blanket static-exercise advice conflicts with later feasibility testing of isometrics (DQT-P1), so it must remain explicitly unresolved.

sources.publicationStatus: Final randomized feasibility trial, Hand Therapy 2023;28(2):72–84.

sources.design: Randomized high-load versus low-load feasibility trial; 28 participants randomized.
sources.population: Adults with probable/almost-certain de Quervain syndrome after two weeks of orthosis, education and ROM. Pregnancy and relevant comorbidities were trial exclusions, not proven universal contraindications.
sources.comparator: 25% versus 70% clinician-measured maximum voluntary isometric contraction; no nonexercise control.
sources.coInterventions: Custom orthosis, individualized education and pain-free active ROM.
sources.outcomes: Pain/function improved over time without group differences; strength/ROM did not improve significantly. Exercise adherence 86.7%.
sources.followUp: Two-week lead-in plus four weeks of loading.
sources.uncertainty: Feasibility does not prove efficacy. No superior load arm; measured force and device calibration matter.
sources.harms: Two exercise-pain reports, including one two-day pause; four minor orthosis events; no serious adverse events.
sources.limitations: 28 adults randomized after 2-week orthosis/education/pain-free-ROM phase to 25% versus 70% maximum voluntary isometric thumb extension, daily for 4 weeks. Five 20-second holds, 1-minute rests; clinician measured force and adjusted weekly. No nonexercise control. Pain/function improved over time, no group superiority; strength/ROM did not improve significantly. Two exercise-pain reports (one paused 2 days); four minor orthosis events, no serious events. Feasibility is not efficacy proof or universal safety. Pregnancy/inflammatory disease and relevant comorbidity exclusions restrict applicability, not establish contraindications. Force-meter/device calibration matters; cannot replace measured MVIC with an invented resistance level.

protocol.execution: Forearm supported on table, hand over edge, wrist neutral, proximal thumb phalanx under padded spring gauge. Unaffected hand loads/unloads gauge and stabilizes base; maintain thumb position against force.
protocol.dose: Five 20-second holds with one-minute rest; 25% or 70% clinician-measured MVIC. Neither load arm proved superior.
protocol.frequency: Once daily for four weeks after two-week lead-in.
protocol.supervision: Weekly clinical MVIC measurement and resistance adjustment; home spring-gauge device.
protocol.progression: Recalculate resistance weekly from current MVIC to maintain assigned percentage.
protocol.stoppingRules: If intolerable, reduce hold duration/increase repetitions; if still intolerable, rest one week then reassess. Repeated intolerance prompted cessation. Trial-specific, not released guidance.
